speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Immigration and Colonization) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Soldier Settlement Act to provide that the period during which payments of arrears or instalments subject to bonus privileges may be made be extended' to the thirty-first day of March, 1938.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Sir Eugene Fiset in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: The amendment to this legislation is very slight. In 1933 legislation was put through the house giving power to apply what was known as the dollar for dollar bonus privilege to soldier settlers in making their payments on lands which they had held from the director of soldier settlement administration. This legislation simply extends the period over which they may take advantage of that privilege from March 31, 1936, to March 31, 1938.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
I have been asked by a body of soldier settlers in the district I represent

to ask if this legislation could not be extended five years. They claim that owing to the depression, which cannot be denied, they have been able to take but comparatively little advantage of the existing act, and that if the extension is for only two years they will find themselves in the same condition two years hence, as there is no possibility of things improving so rapidly as to enable them to get ahead to meet these payments. They ask if it could not be arranged now to extend the period for five years, so that they would have something definite towards which they could work, and make their arrangements accordingly.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: I think there is something to be said for that request, but after giving consideration to the question of extension for a longer period we decided that perhaps on the whole it would be best to ask for only two years' extension. If the conditions that exist two years from now make it advisable to extend the period for another year, or two or three years, it can always be done by a very simple amendment to the act. On the other hand I think it is desirable that those who are in a position to make payments should make them, and I do not think any very serious injury will be done to those for whom the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) speaks by enacting into law the measure as it now stands. It can always be further extended should that be considered desirable.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: As I understand it, the soldier settler who pays one dollar gets credit for an additional dollar on his indebtedness; that is the effect of the existing legislation.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES

speechtext: Has the minister available the number who have taken advantage of the legislation, and the amounts paid in, by provinces?

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
I am afraid I have not
before me a note of the number who have taken, advantage of it. It has been operative from 1933, when the legislation was passed, until March 31 of the present year, 1936. During that time payments received subject to bonus from the soldier settlers were 82,430,660.22. The bonus credited to date on those payments amounts to SI,648,485.14. There was a provison in the legislation passed in 1933 that before a soldier could avail himself of the bonus privilege he had to have his taxes and his insurance paid; consequently there' is a further amount of $782,175.80 to be credited when taxes and insurance are paid. The experience in the administration, I am told by the officials, is that where the soldiers

Soldier Settlement Act
could take advantage of it, that is where they had some crops, where they had some income which provided them with cash in hand to take advantage of it, they did so. Cases where this could not be done were those where crops suffered severely from drought or rust or other adverse conditions, and their income was insufficient to enable them to take advantage of the legislation. We hope by extending it for two years to enable them to take advantage of the provision that was embodied in the legislation of 1933.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES

If my memory serves me rightly, the total that is now considered possible of collection is around 850,000,000. I mention that figure, however, subject to correction.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
May I say, there is
an organization of soldier settlers throughout western Canada known as the soldier settlers' union. The members of that union appreciate very much the legislation that was passed recently and is being amended this year by the government, but tiheir opinion, as I understand it, is that the legislation, though very needful, does not go far enough. I should like to put before the minister that point of view, and the request of the members of that organization that they be given an opportunity to confer with the minister some time during the present year to discuss further aspects of the soldier settlement question in western Canada. In other words, they would like to bring before the minister, the total debt of the soldier settlers, the interest on that debt, the annual amount of that interest and how they might be enabled to meet it in the years to come. They feel that the time has come when perhaps the interest payments should be given up entirely and the principal so arranged that they may be able to meet their obligations year by year over a stated period. May I ask, then, if the minister would be favourable to having a conference with the representatives of this union and of the veterans who are also interested in this vital matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
I would not object to meeting with the organization to which my hon. friend refers, but I am not familiar with it and I do not know how representative it is. After all, these soldier settlers cover a very wide area, and I do not know that any particular advantage would be gained if the
organization to which my hon. friend refers is more or less local in character. Of course the legion have been interested in the welfare of the returned soldiers on the land as well as the welfare of other returned soldiers, and I think I am correct in saying that the measure I am now asking the committee to approve has been approved by the legion. As I said a moment ago, I have no objection to sitting down with any interests representing the returned soldiers, but I think it only reasonable to say that in any case these interests should be representative. If this is a representative organization embracing the whole dominion I shall be very glad to sit down and discuss the whole matter with them.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: No, it does not represent the whole dominion, although I believe there is a certain membership scattered throughout the country. It particularly represents the three western provinces, and the members of that union frel that they should be given an opportunity to cooperate with the veterans in any meeting the minister may arrange. That is the position in a nutshell.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
I am very glad to endorse the suggestion just made by the hon. member for North Battleford (Mr. McIntosh). I think there are many cases in western Canada that should be reconsidered, in which there really should be revaluations. The legislation passed in 1933 was very favourably received, and at that time the soldier settlers thought it would be of great benefit to them. However, owing to the continuous crop failures in certain parts of the west many of these returned men have had nothing for five years, certainly nothing to apply on a dollar for dollar bonus scheme. The minister has mentioned the amount that has been credited under this act since 1933, something around $1,500,000, and when you compare that sum with the total yet outstanding that the minister states may be collected, amounting to some $50,000,000, it will be seen that the soldier settlers have not been able to do very much even under that legislation. I do not say there should be a general revaluation, but in many cases even after what has been done in the past the land is still valued too highly. These men want to pay for their land, I know; many of them have married since taking up this land and I know they are anxious to meet their obligations and make their permanent homes there. I am glad to see this amendment brought down, but I agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that two years is not going to be long enough.
Soldier Settlement Act

I trust that, as the minister has said, the government will grant a further extension if necessary when the time comes.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: May I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the discussion is getting perhaps a little out of order. After all we are considering the extension of this period for bonus payments. The matters that have been brought up by my hon. friends from North Battleford and Qu'Appelle could be discussed when the estimates of the soldier settlement board are before the committee, when all the information will be available on the points they have raised. If I might offer a suggestion it would be that we confine the discussion to this particular point.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: While what the minister says is quite true, I am of the opinion that a two year extension will not meet the case. The fact that the extension is for only two years means that in the meantime a number of these soldier settlers will be consumed with anxiety from time to time. I should like to see the minister and the committee take a more realistic view of the situation and make this extension for a much longer period. I would suggest also that in the meantime the point raised by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle be taken into consideration and that a revaluation of much of this land be undertaken. I know from personal experience, as I am sure many other hon. members know, that the condition of many of these settlers in th'e dried out areas and the bush country of western Canada is deplorable. I know that people who have looked into their situation realize that they are in a hopeless position at the present time. I suggest to the minister, therefore, that this extension be for more than two years and that in the meantime a thorough survey be made of soldier settlements with a view to determining what lands are submarginal and upon what lands it may be possible for returned men to meet the payments that will come due in the future, because I am quite sure that in many instances the condition of such settlers is quite hopeless.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
I desire to keep myself strictly to the subject of the resolution. I think it is desirable that this legislation should be extended for some period, because many men have not been able to take advantage of the bonus, for two reasons, the failure of the crops and the exceedingly low prices that have been realized. I have the honour of representing probably the largest number of soldier settlers in any constituency in the province of Saskatchewan,

and from time to time they have made representations to me. They favour having this plan extended for another year. In the first place they asked me to have it extended until the end of this fiscal year, until the spring time. Later they asked that it be extended for another year and then from year to year, as, if and when necessary, as conditions developed. There are two views held with regard to extending it for one or for five years. The returned soldiers who spoke to me wanted it extended from year to year, * while some others would like to have it extended for five years. Many of those men who are settlers themselves do not ask that it be extended for five years at a time, because then the 'human desire to procrastinate enters into the question. If it is known that one has five years in which to make payment he will probably think he might as well do as some of us have done with our life insurance premiums and such matters, delay and delay, until the sum becomes too large; whereas if it has to be paid within a year there is more likelihood that the payment will be made promptly if means are available. For that reason I support the action of the minister in asking that the time be extended for two years, although, as I say, I have been asked to see that it be extended if possible from year to year unless conditions make any further extensions unnecessary.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
I wish to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. McLean). I think the government are wise in extending the period for two years only. We are only human, and that applies to returned soldiers as well as to others; some of them might be inclined to postpone their payments, even if they were in a position to meet them, if they thought they had at least five years within which to make good. It seems to me that the extension for two years only will have the effect of inducing them to make their payments more promptly. The suggestion of the minister is,
I understand, that if at the end of two years conditions are such as to require it, the term can be again extended. That seems to me the proper procedure and one which will work no hardship on the returned men. While I have not a large number of soldier settlers in my riding, I have some; I have had requests from these men that the government extend the time for taking advantage of this legislation, and I know they will be grateful to the government for doing so.
I should like at the same time to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member

Soldier Settlement Act
for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley).
I think there are many cases where the situation should be reviewed to see whether these men are placed on land on which they can make a living. I know for a fact that the best farmers in this country could not make a living on some of the land on which soldier settlers were placed. I have in mind a man who worked all summer for a neighbour of mine.
I was loading a car of wheat with him last fall and he told me this story: "I am married;
I have two children, but my wife and children are home with her parents and I am working out here." I said, "Did you never settle on the land?" He said, "Yes, but from the land I settled on no man could make a living." He said he had applied for land that was suitable but his application was refused. I am not personally acquainted with the facts, but that is what he told me. Some provision should be made for a man like that who wants to get on the land and establish a home. We talk about the unemployed drifting into our cities, and we know they should remain on the land if possible. This is one instance, which could be multiplied by thousands, and the government should undertake to review such cases, as suggested by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. I commend the government for the action they have taken, and believe this bill is worthy of our favourable consideration.
. Mr. YOUNG: Does the dollar for dollar provision in the act apply to the soldier settler's total indebtedness, that is to both principal and interest?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: No, it applies to all the payments made between the date of coming into force of the act passed in 1933, and March 31, 1936. This amendment extends that period for two years, consequently it will apply to all payments made between the date of coming into force of the act and March 31, 1938. If the soldier settler is in arrears for two or three years he can pay up the arrears and get the advantage of the dollar for dollar bonus on payments made during this period.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext:
Just a word in connection with the two points I tried to emphasize. The first is that the legislation before the committee is on the whole satisfactory to the soldier settlers throughout western Canada. If there is occasion to extend it in the future it can be extended when the time comes, but this extension for two years is being accepted by them in the right spirit and they feel that it is a move in the right direction.
The other point to which I referred was to a conference between the minister or the
department and representatives of soldier settlers and veterans generally. My point is that any matter pertaining to soldier settlers in western Canada with regard to interest and debt could be brought up and discussed. Then if it is thought wise to have a survey made, that can be done, but my intention in mentioning a conference was to have all questions that require consideration presented and reviewed there and not necessarily discussed in the house at the present time.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: Could the minister give the percentage of returned soldier settlers who took advantage of this legislation? If he has the figures for each province I would appreciate it.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: I regret that I cannot give the number by provinces; the information I have here does not enable me to answer the question. But I shall make a note of it, and we shall try to have the information available when we are considering the item in the estimates that deals with soldier settlement.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: It is the resolution we are discussing now; perhaps the minister could give it on the bill.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: I think I can get that. It is not material, but I think I can get it.

subtopic: EXTENSION OF TIME FOR PAYMENTS OF ARREARS OR INSTALMENTS SUBJECT TO BONUS PRIVILEGES
speechtext: I commend the action of the minister in extending this period for two years, but I know that is not enough. The suggestion that a revaluation should be made should not be lost sight of. In my district I know one man who bought a half section of land and some horses and machinery. The original price was $8,000. and to-day I understand he owes $13,000 on that outfit. Those who were fortunate enough to start in far better circumstances than that man are still suffering under some handicap, and I cannot see how he will ever get out of the mire that he is pressed into to-day, not because he is not a good farmer but because of the situation he is up against. The dominion promised to take care of the men they sent overseas, and the way it is hanging a burden of debt around the necks of the men who returned is not right. They went through enough when they were overseas, and Canada should do its share and at least not place a millstone around their necks. There should be a revaluation.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Superintendent General of Indian Affairs) moved the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the Indian Act.

Is the minister going to
speak? If not, I should like to say a few words.

The minister
ought to give an explanation indicating what the bill is to cover.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I shall be glad to do so.
A brief explanation was given when the resolution preceding the bill came before the house.

Then let us
have a fuller explanation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I shall endeavour to meet
the very reasonable request of the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley).
The amendments contained in the bill cover several matters relating to Indian administration.. Section 1 of the bill deals with property left as the result of the death of an Indian on a reserve. At the present time he cannot leave such property to any person outside the reserve, and there is a provision in the Indian Act for the disposal of such property to some individual resident on the reserve. The amendment provides that the band may purchase such property out of band funds.
The next section deals with the protection of fruit trees and orchards on reserves. I believe there are a few instances in British Columbia where orchards exist on reserves adjacent to other communities in which the chief occupation is the production of fruit. At the present time there are no provisions in the Indian Act to compel the spraying of orchards on reserves, and under the amendment power is sought to have such provision. Then, certain powers are sought in connection with the control of motor vehicle traffic on the reserves.
The next section of the bill gives the band the right to purchase the property to which reference is made in the first section.

The next section deals with decisions at meetings of the council of the band. Very often the Indian agent is the presiding officer, and in the bill there is a provision under which the person presiding at such meeting may have the casting vote, if such is necessary.
The next section deals with the procedure which shall be followed at meetings of the council of the band.
In regard to the amendment in clause 6 of the bill, it may be noted that the sections in the present act relating to the subject are to the effect that if any person is found in possession of an intoxicant in the house, wigwam or place of abode of an Indian, certain penalties will follow. The relevant section of the present bill provides that if he has such intoxicant in a hotel room, being occupied by an Indian, he is subject to the same penalties that would apply if he had the intoxicant in the Indian's tent or wigwam.
There are several sections in the Indian Act under which an informer is entitled to a moiety of the fines collected. We propose to repeal that provision by striking out in each of the sections indicated in the bill the provision which gives the informer a part of the fine which may be assessed against the person infringing the act.
Would the minister enlarge upon the reasons for this radical change?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The change is suggested mainly from British Columbia. I am told the attorney general of that province has expressed himself as being favourable to it. Many of our Indian agents and others who have been associated with Indian administration in the province, or matters having to do with Indians, have also suggested that this would be a desirable amendment. That is why it is included in the bill.
The next section relates to what is known as the potlatch. I regret I am unable to give the house a learned dissertation on the potlatch, but apparently it is a kind of Indian festival dating back a long time. The best information I can get about it indicates that many generations ago it was the occasion of Indians meeting to carry on a certain amount of public business. As they had no writings they desired to have as many witnesses as possible to the conclusions or decisions reached. This practice persisted down through the years, but like many similar institutions among other races of men it changed as the years passed, with the result that now, except possibly in one district of British Columbia, the potlatch has ceased to exist. The IndiaD

Indian Act-Mr. Neill
Act contains rather stringent provisions against it. The amendments provided by the bill are simply to enlarge the restrictive provisions, in the expectation that it will assist in doing away with this ceremony even in the more remote parts in which I am informed it still persists.
The next clause has to do with the residence qualifications of an Indian councillor. Formerly the councillor had to be possessed of and had to live in a house on the reserve. The proposed amendment enables the councillor to qualify on being possessed of a house on the reserve and living thereon, without having to live in that particular house.
What I have said covers briefly, and, I hope, adequately, the purposes of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, the provisions of this bill are all appropriate and necessary, I think, with the exception of two. Sections 7 to 12 propose to abolish giving a moiety of a fine to the informer. There may be the objection which the minister has stated or which is set out on the explanatory page of the bill, that it leads to men being too anxious to dig up an offence in order to collect half the fine. But I would hesitate to say that the giving of this moiety should be done away with. It has been in force for a great many years and I think has been very seldom abused. I have seen attempts made to abuse it. I have seen an Indian go out and pay ten dollars for a bottle of whiskey and have a drunk on it. He then laid an information against the man who sold him the whiskey; the seller would be fined fifty dollars, of which the Indian got twenty-five, and thereby was created a revolving fund with which to continue the operation. But no sensible official or magistrate would permit such a thing for a moment. I was Indian agent for ten years, and if I saw any disposition of that kind I remedied it simply by seeing that someone other than such a gentleman was the informant. A policeman could be the informant-he would not get half the fine-or anyone else. In these out of the way places the law is administered with not exactly the same severity and accuracy as to technicalities that prevails, say, in the Supreme Court of Canada, and there are occasions on which an informer does require some compensation. A rather decent Indian in a band may take it upon himself to try to suppress the liquor business, and it is only fair that he should get some compensation for the trouble he takes. Very often he may have to go a good many miles in a canoe to attend court, and so on, and it is desirable to have this money under the hand of
the magistrate by means of which he may deal out rough and ready justice. I recall a case many years ago in which a white man had seduced an Indian woman; to that end he made the husband1 drunk, and the Indian went away and fell into the water and was drowned. It was up to me to handle the situation. I could not see that sending the man to gaol was going to do any particular good-he had a wife and family and some position-nor would it have done the widow much good, so I stretched the law perhaps a little in fining him some ridiculously large sum, I think $500. I put in the widow as the informant, by which she got $250, and I kept that in hand and fed it out to her at so much a month for a couple of years, by which time she had got married again and everybody was more or less satisfied. That was rough and ready justice which would not have met with the approval perhaps of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), but it was the sort of thing that was needed in these out of the way places.
The other provision to which I take very definite objection is the one proposing to increase the penalty in connection with potlatching. This is a practice that occurs in the district that I represent, and therefore it is up to me to give expression to the views of some of the Indians who have written to me on the subject. Unfortunately there appeared in the press at the time notice was given of the provisions of this bill, comment upon this practice of potlatching. It said that the Indians were in the habit of going to great excesses, going so far even as to give away their squaws. The minister's name unfortunately was used in the same paragraph, and it rather conveyed the suggestion that he was responsible for the statement in the press. The Indians were very much upset and four of the chiefs in the district wrote me. Commenting on this newspaper item they say:
It has never been the custom to indulge in any of -the practices mentioned, such as giving away our wives, and we whose names are subscribed have never heard of its being done, and we consider a great wrong has been done to our people in charging this against us. We still give away presents at some parties, but in no instance does the donor beggar himself or involve his family, as was formerly the custom. With our education and other benefits conferred on us by the government, these ancient customs, that is the injurious ones, are rapidly dying out naturally. As most of us have been baptized, confirmed and married in the church, we feel that a great injustice has been done in accusing us of giving away our wives at a potlatch. We also consider that someone has been violating the ninth commandment in accusing us of such a practice. We wish you would do what you can to put this matter in its true light.
12S8
Indian Act-Mr. Neill

I leave it to the minister to locate the ninth commandment, as I am not as familiar with it as I might be. I do not want to go into a dissertation on the potlatch, but putting it briefly, it has a very old origin. The Indians got together and had a potlatch for the inauguration of the young men of the band, and there was a ceremony in which a living dog was hung up and the candidate for admission to the band had to take bites out of this living animal. That is already prohibited by law. But what is now more properly called the potlatch consists in an Indian who wishes to get a high standing among his fellow men collecting a large quantity of goods-it may be flour, potatoes, anything at all-and then he calls together the band, or a whole band may give a potlatch, a communal affair, at which everything will be given away. I have seen men give away the very beds they slept on and the stoves they wanted to cook with. They did not give away their women; the trouble was, the use they would put their women to in order to get the cash to give the potlatch. But that practice gradually died away. The influence of the white man induced an individualism amongst the Indians, and I was careful to instil that point of view myself when I was Indian agent. I used to point out to them that it left them in poverty. But there was another aspect; in one sense it was a sort of old age pension insurance scheme. A hearty young man in the prime of life who gave one of these potlatches had certainly to include all the old people when giving away the gifts; therefore they got a return on the money they had invested in potlatches in the past, and it worked well in that way. Of course, nowadays with Indian agents handing out relief it is not so necessary, and the practice is dying out. The Indians are getting away from that point of view.
As the minister has said, a very stringent law was passed about the matter. I am not kicking about its stringency, but I object to its extension. The present law provides that anyone who takes part in a potlatch is liable to imprisonment for not less than two months and not exceeding six months, which is a very severe penalty to impose on a savage when you are trying to wean him away from his ancient habits and rights, from the Indian point of view. I have had Indians say to me, as a white man, "Do you not gather your friends together at Christmas and give them presents? Then why should we not do the same?" I remember on one occasion some over-zealous individual reported me to 
Ottawa for having allowed a potlatch at a certain place. I went down to see what the trouble was, and it turned out that the Indians had had some kind of pageant, got up by some of the children attending school. In the pageant a whale appeared and all of a sudden burst asunder and a lot of young fellows dressed in white stepped out, and there were other appropriate scenes. Fortunately someone had taken a picture of it, which I sent to Ottawa. I said in making my report to Ottawa that the night before the potlatch I had attended a fancy dress ball in the place in which I live; that the first prize had gone to a man who represented a monkey, and that I could not see much difference between representing a monkey and representing a whale, the preference being rather in favour of the whale as there had been more ingenuity and more painstaking preparations for its appearance. In that way, by not putting my foot down and sending these Indians to gaol, but rather looking at it sympathetically, no harm was done. I did not prosecute any of the Indians.
The potlatch still exists in the district referred to in this bill. I think that given a little time, and dealing with the Indians reasonably instead of going at them in such an unfair way as indicated here, any evil that may exist will die out. I am not thoroughly familiar with the situation but I suggest that a little more care might be taken by the officials in enforcing the present law, instead of making it more drastic. We do not want to be put in the position of that sultan who, when a baker was brought before him for having given false weight in his bread, put the baker himself in the oven and baked him and boasted that he had put an end to the matter. That is not the method we want to pursue here.
It is provided here, in addition to the already stringent features, that any man who takes part in a festival any part of w'hich consists in the giving away of articles shall go to gaol for six months, and now he is to go to gaol if he has been saving, storing or accumulating any goods or articles for the purpose of giving them away. Who shall read into a man's mind to decide what his purpose is when he accumulates earthly goods? He may be accumulating them to leave them to his grandchildren; or as Joseph and the Israelites of old, who in the good years stored up provisions against the depression, this Indian may foresee a depression and decide to store up certain things against a rainy day. But somebody or other not defined, the informer maybe or the magistrate, may think that the Indian intends to give away the things he is storing

Indian Act-Mr. Woodsworth
up; somebody may be of the opinion that he is going to give them away before, after or at such celebration, mark you. Well, when can he store them up? Never at all; because there is no period in human life which is not before, at the time of or after a particular deed or event. I think that is going beyond reason. Would the department care to apply such provisions to white people? That is the test. I note further a trifling detail that indicates sloppy legislation; it speaks of any goods or articles of any sort suspected of being about to he given. How can you suspect an inanimate object? Here is a desk; I may suspect the owner of the desk of having done something with it, but it is not open for me in law to suspect the desk of being about to be done something to. This language ought to read, "the owner of which is suspected."
This legislation is uncalled for. The act is stringent enough and it has been effective, and the necessity for its enforcement is becoming less and less. Will the minister's officials say that the evil is increasing? I venture to say it is not. I rather think that they desire to avoid a little trouble in enforcing the law as it stands, by having a law which will be automatic, so that they may come along at any time and say that it is in this or that man's mind to do so and so. The minister might well consider the advisability of leaving that part of the act as it is for a few years longer. Has he any evidence from his officials to the effect that this evil is getting substantially worse than it has been in years gone by?

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
speechtext:
I wish to express my sympathy with the point of view put forward by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). In the course of my life, most of which has been spent in the west, I have had the opportunity on a number of occasions of coming more or less in contact with the Indians, and I do believe we ought not to be too stringent in these regulations that are laid down or in these acts that are from time to time brought before the house. I suggest, though not with respect to these particular clauses of the bill, that we should have a larger measure of consultation between the department and the Indians themselves. I know tihat the Indians are wards of the government; but they are also recognized as having a government of their own: they are at one and the same time within Canada and yet a sort of imperium in imperio. They have certain rights of their own, certain forms of organization, and these are recognized. I have come across a number of instances where the department is too far removed from the
Indians, and the local agent is a little too arrogant, with the result that there are a great many misunderstandings between the white people and the Indians. I do not know the Indians of eastern Canada but I can imagine that if there were new regulations that insisted that the Indians should spray their orchards or should conform to provincial regulations in force among the white people, there would be a great deal of difficulty. I am not blaming the white people for wanting to prevent the spread of disease into their orchards; but I do say that there ought to be some recognized method of consultation with the Indians when new regulations of this kind are being introduced. Before an act of this kind is passed there ought to be a conference between the Indians and the department. The whole matter ought to be very clearly set forth so that when the act actually comes into force the Indians will know what it is all about.
We take it for granted that ignorance of an act is no excuse, but in the case of Indians it may be a very real excuse. They ought to know all that is involved in these acts and ought to be helped to reconcile the difference that exists between their mode of life and that of the whites. It is only within the last few days that I have been consulted with regard to certain rights of Indians on lands on which prospecting is now done for minerals and gas. I think a great many of the Indians hardly know what their rights are. It is not very easy for them to consult lawyers as to those rights, and I venture to say that a good many of the lawyers would have to spend a considerable time before they understood exactly what the rights of the Indians were both as bands and as individual Indians within those bands. I venture to bring this matter to the attention of the minister, who I am sure is sympathetic to the Indians. As the Indians are more and more encompassed with white civilization, we might work out something of a new technique of consultation between Indian bands and the department before such regulations are definitely brought into force.

I am not directly or personally interested in the affairs of the Indians, but I am always interested in the affairs of any people who in my opinion are not getting a square deal. My hon. friend has said that the Indians of Canada are the wards of the government. It is natural then to assume that the government should take care of them. I am personally affected in that respect to this extent. The city I represent is just now and has been for the last four years supplementing the
Indian Act-Mr. Pelletier

government's grant to the Indians by taking care of a considerable number of Indian families in Hamilton-families who leave their reservations not far from the city and move in and become a charge on the city. If the government is responsible for the maintenance of the Indians, I suggest that it give them adequate sustenance so that this extra burden will not be placed on the cities. As I say, the city of Hamilton for the past four years has been supplementing the government's grants by taking care of Indian families. Why they are not forced to remain on their lands, the government taking care of them in the proper way, I am not able to understand. It would seem to me that the department could well investigate this particular situation through their government inspectors or Indian agents and bring the Indians who have gone into the cities back to the reserves where they belong, where they can be kept, and properly kept. After all they are the only real Canadians we have, and it is the duty of this government to see that they are taken care of under government supervision and do not become part of the obligation placed on urban centres throughout Ontario and throughout Canada.

There is an Indian reserve within my constituency, and because of that fact I have had occasion to come in contact with Indians from time to time. I am very much pleased to see that the duties of the agents in so far as the election of chiefs is concerned have been thoroughly defined. I suggest that we could possibly go a bit further than that. I gather from the remarks of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) that some of the Indians are not always cognizant of the law, and that perhaps, since they do not know the law, they are not responsible for breaking it. The explanatory note to section 13 of the bill states that section 140, subsection 1, prohibits what is known as the potlatch, a ceremony peculiar to the Indians of the west coast of British Columbia; that this subsection in one form or another has been in the Indian Act for over fifty years, and was introduced at the request of the Indians themselves, "particularly the more progressive elements." I should like to make special reference to that last sentence. It seems to me that immediately a chief is elected he should become the subject of special attention by the Indian agent or the Indian department. We know that the more progressive elements are pressing for progressive legislation. I do not know, of course, whether this condition exists all over Canada, but I do know that in certain tribes the chief

is not really qualified to act as such. I believe he should receive the special consideration of the department and should be given a certain amount of education which would fit him to administer the affairs of his tribe in a satisfactory manner.
I should also like to suggest that influence be brought to bear to promote the election of younger men as chiefs of tribes. I received not long ago a letter from one of the Indians living on a reservation in my constituency in which he related to me a visit he had just paid to the chief of his tribe. He told me that the chief was quite an old man, that apparently he could not get about very much and could not very well take care of himself, and that it did not have a very good effect on the other Indians when they found out that he had practically nothing to eat in the place he lived in; it seemed to carry the impression that these people are not looked after.
His wigwam.

Possibly, his wigwam. Of course I have never lived there and I do not know what it would be like. The impression was that the chief was not very well looked after. I believe that a person in his position should be enabled to act as a real connecting link between the Indians themselves and the Indian agent. If he were capable of administering the affairs of the tribe in a more efficient manner the results to the Indians themselves would be very beneficial, and possibly by his good business management the necessity would be avoided of laws going so far as even to suppose what is in the minds of certain people.
I think that the chief should be the subject of special consideration. So far as possible he should be young, and once he is elected he should be given a certain amount of education in the matter of administering the affairs of his tribe, so that he may be able properly to represent to the agent the demands of the Indians, to settle troubles from time to time, and to give a good example to his tribe.

I am interested in any questions affecting the Indians, because there is a reserve in my constituency. In the first place I should like to reply to the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mr. Wilton) with regard to a situation that has developed in some of our cities adjacent to the reserve which I happen to represent; there have been complaints because some of our Indians have gone to live in the city. The late government introduced a compulsory enfranchisement act which I am inclined to think was a mistake

Indian Act-Mr. Wood
I may enlarge on that later. Indians had been enabled to collect from their capital funds, the band funds, that portion which belonged to themselves and their families. They would get it in cash, having become to all intents and purposes Canadian citizens and assumed the rights and obligations of citizenship. In prosperous times advantage was taken of that provision by some families, members of the band. In one particular case to which my attention has been drawn, the Indian with his wife and family collected considerably over
SI,000	in the way of a capital fund. It happened that the family consisted largely of daughters, and it was less than five years before five of these daughters married Indians, and were back in the Indian reserve, residing there by virtue of the fact that they married men of their own race. They had the advantage of spending these band funds; now they are back upon the Indian reserve, and the result is that the band funds are depleted by just that amount. The hon. member for Hamilton West must remember that to all intents and purposes they are Canadian citizens, and, while they are enfranchised, are just as much entitled to relief in the cities as any other Canadian citizen or any person of foreign birth who has Canadian citizenship rights. I rather think that compulsory enfranchisement is wrong, and I would make a protest against the further enforcement of that act.
I was interested in the remarks of the hon. member for (Comox-Alberni) Mr. Neill, and particularly his comments on the festivities. I do not think the government need have any undue concern with regard to those festivities, because they are gradually dying out. Of course the Indians guard very jealously some of their traditions. On our Indian reserve a feast takes place every year which is called the burning of the white dog. It sounds very vicious, but the fact of the matter is that they do not burn a white dog. It has developed into more or less of a social affair, they have a program arranged; they are very glad to have visitors from any section, and on a particular evening when they are having their war dances if you happen to go there you will have to dance whether you know how to do it or not. The point is that they enjoy these things, and I think they are beginning to get on a higher plane; their old traditions are being woven into our civilization. I am not so sure that we need be much concerned about placing restrictions on them, though we may correct such errors as happen to exist among them.
I quite understand that the minister has had a great deal of difficulty in trying to draft a 12739-83
law that will take into consideration all the irregularities that exist in Indian reserves, because there are very great differences in the types of these Indians and in regard to the band funds. I would recommend to the department that, wherever possible, they extend the autonomy of the Indians and give them more right to discharge their own affairs. I take the same view in connection with Indians that I take in connection with ourselves; the less government interference we have in many things the more chance there is to create individual initiative, and I think that is one of the fundamentals we must observe on the road to recovery. We can do a great deal to encourage our Indians to develop their own initiative, and I believe that will help them out of many of their difficulties.
With regard to the education of their chiefs or rulers, I think that must be left to each individual reserve. The group I have the honour to represent are perhaps among the most advanced in the country, and I wish to place myself on record as believing that they could be given almost complete autonomy. I believe they are quite capabie of discharging their own business. I think the township of Tuscarora, which is inhabited completely by the Six Nations Indians, should be incorporated in the county of Brant. Let them administer their own affairs, elect their own council and pay their share of the cost of the administration of justice in the county, as other townships do. I have no qualms of conscience in making that suggestion, and I hope and trust the Indian department may see its way clear to take some such action in order to encourage the Indians to assume full responsibility just as quickly as their advance in civilization will permit. We have an Indian superintendent in Brantford to administer the affairs of the Indians, but I believe the people on this reserve have enough ability to administer their own affairs, and in that way perhaps the government could save some money. I am quite conscious of the importance of the statement I am making, but I make it in all sincerity because I believe these Indians have the ability to do as I have suggested. I would ask the department, instead of retarding their progress by taking away their responsibilities, as we have done in connection with their education, to endeavour to have them undertake greater responsibility as I have suggested. Only eleven years ago they instituted an elective system for the selection of their council, the same system that is followed in every other municipality; in fact they do some things that I think might well be done in some of

Indian Act

the other municipalities. I would ask the department to give serious consideration to the suggestions I have advanced.
