speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are no longer wards of the nation.
Do I understand the Minister of Justice to say that when an Indian becomes enfranchised he has ceased to be an Indian?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, I think so.
Well, that is news to me.

I think the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. YVoodsworth) has not considered the point that probably the reason for the provision was the special
temperament and special characteristics pertaining only to Indians. The Indian is of such a temperament that he may be more easily influenced or stimulated by intoxicants than other inhabitants of the country, generally speaking, and these provisions are put in the act for his protection. Whether hebe on his own reservation or in a private room at a hotel his makeup or temperament would still be Indian, and, as the government has^ attempted to do, he must be protected against himself irrespective of his location at the time he becomes intoxicated.
Does he lose that temperatment when he takes Canadian citizenship?

Certainly not; nobody contends that. The hon. gentleman should not interpret my remarks in that way. I say that he is still an Indian, and retains the temperament and makeup of the Indian. Under those circumstances he is entitled to and must have the protection of those of whom he is a ward.
The argument supports my contention. He would not get the protection, under the interpretation given by the Minister of Justice, because according to the minister he ceases to be an Indian.
He comes under ordinary laws.

I have no particular fault to find with the object behind the proposed change. I believe it is a good thing for those Indians who are wards of the government. We must remember however that as soon as an Indian becomes naturalized he does not come under the provisions of this section.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He does not come under the provisions of the act.

There is another class of Indians which I believe should be considered. Although they are not very great in number, they have rights and privileges which they have won; I refer to the Indians who fought overseas in the great war. They have been given rights of citizenship so far as the vote is concerned. They say they were good enough to fight for their country and that to all intents and purposes they are citizens of Canada, and even though they may still be wards of the government they feel that they should be exempted from this clause. I point that out to the minister and ask him to give it his consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I call attention of the hon. member for Winni-
*1296

Indian Act
-peg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) to section 110 of the Indian Act, paragraph 5, which says:
On the report of the Superintendent General that any Indian, male or female, over the age of twenty-one years is fit for enfranchisement, the governor in council may by order direct that such Indian shall be and become enfranchised at the expiration of two years from the date of such order or earlier if requested by such Indian, and from the date of such enfranchisement the provisions of this and ot any other act or law making any distinction between the legal rights, privileges, disabilities and liabilities of Indians and those of His Majesty's other subjects, shall cease to apply to such Indian or to his or her minor unmarried children, or, in the case of a married male Indian, to the wife of such Indian, and every such Indian and child and wife shall thereafter have, possess and enjoy all the legal powers, rights and privileges of His Majesty s other subjects, and shall no longer be deemed to be Indians within the meaning of any laws relating to Indians.
So that I was right, and these men have the same rights as my hon. friend and myself.
I am quite willing to admit that the law is beyond the comprehension of ordinary mortals.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Sections 7 to 11 inclusive agreed to.
On section 12-Intoxicants at council or meeting.

Before all these clauses are carried, I would ask the minister if his officials and those in the department who have been at this work for years and understand the Indians better than most ^ of us do, are definitely in favour of this being done? Is it being done on their recommendation, or at whose request?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I can say definitely that it is being done on their recommendation made to me. As I have already confessed, I have not been very long in charge of the department, but with the supporting evidence that was presented to me I approve of the general principle of these amendments.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section	13-Celebrating	festivities,
dances or ceremonies at which presents are made, or bodies mutilated.
Will the minister give us some information on this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I listened with a great deal of interest to the observations made by the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) when he was discussing this section earlier in the afternoon. The section comes
IMr. E. Lapointe.]
to me recommended by the officers of the department. The committee will observe, and I think my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi will agree, that the amendment simply extends a principle that is already in the section. The potlatch I think practically has ceased to be carried on in its original form in all but one or two agencies in British Columbia. My hon. friend is quite right in the statement he made in the discussion on the second reading of the bill this afternoon, that the potlatch custom is dying out among the Indians. But it does persist, I am informed, in one particular agency, and this amendment seeks to draw a little tighter the provision that has been in the law for the last fifty years, and which was put in the law, I am informed, originally at the request of the Indians themselves, in order if possible to put a stop to this practice. I think this amendment might be given a chance to operate. It will be enforced as reasonably as possible, and it may be that its very presence in the law will be a sufficient deterrent to the Indians who still desire to carry on this practice.

Mr. Chairman, I would rather have expected to hear some evidence in the direction that the practice was increasing and doing more harm and taking place oftener than before, but evidently that is not the fact. The minister agrees that the custom is dying out, that the law as it at present exists has worked successfully. Then why alter it? The practice is dying out; there is no increase of it. Why seek to speed the process up by the insertion of a provision in the law which is unjust? If this provision were applied to me I would be inspired with a desire to go out and do this very thing, just to show that I had the right to do it. You say here that a man shall be put in peril of his liberty for six months because someone in office thinks the Indian has it in his mind to do something. Who can tell what is in any man's mind? The clause cannot be invoked except on the presumption that the man is storing up goods for the purpose of giving them away in an illegitimate way. Now, how can you tell that? It is an unjust provision. The minister suggests that it will be used with discretion. I would say the only discretion you can use about it would be to ignore it altogether. The fact of the matter is, and I am driven more and more to this conclusion because we have no evidence presented to show that the practice is increasing, I believe this provision is being put in the law because someone wants us to do his work for him. He won't go out and hunt

Indian Act
up the evidence. He would have it made a criminal offence if a man had it in his mind to do these things, he being the judge as to whether he had it in his mind or not to do something at a future time. I remember once when I was a magistrate a man was to be brought	before	me, and	the	policemansaid,	"He is	a bad	man and	I want you tosoak	it to	him."	I asked	the	policeman,"How many times has he been convicted of this offence?" "None at all," was the reply, "but	he has been	doing it	for	years." I
said, "So far as I am concerned, in this trial the man comes before me for the first time as an innocent man, and if you have neglected your duty and have not taken the trouble to watch him and get evidence against him before, I am not going to make an example of him just because you think he is a bad man." If the minister had produced evidence that the practice was increasing, the situation wmuld have been different, but he has not done so, and the practice is not increasing.
I know the place the minister has in mind, a place called Alert Bay. There are policemen stationed there; an Indian agent lives there; there are uniformed provincial police there, well qualified to take care of any infraction of the law in this direction. I am not arguing that we should do away with the present law, stringent as it is, and enforced for many years, and according to the minister himself enforced successfully. What I am objecting to is increasing the penalty and putting in a provision which I say is unreasonable, unjust and un-British. You might as well pull a man up, declare him to be, guilty, and allow him to prove his innocence. That is always the device of people who do not want to take the trouble of following the ordinaiy procedure of law enforcement; they want to put a man in the box and let him prove his innocence. The Indian is going to be penalized because he is supposed to have in mind the doing of something. He is accumulating goods before, after or at the potlatch, accumulating them for the purpose of giving them away. Why, with such a provision a vindictive man might send any Indian to gaol; for there is no alternative; he cannot get off with a fine, because he is liable on summary conviction to imprisonment for a term not exceeding six months and not less than two months. And he is liable to this penalty for merely saving, storing up or accumulating goods or articles for the purpose of giving them away. That is not a criminal offence, but it is the offence which is here stated. I suppose the minister has introduced this bill on the
advice of his officials. I say to him that the day will come when he will admit that he has been ill advised.

The law as it stands enacts that every Indian who engages in a ceremony of which the giving away of money, goods or articles of any sort, before, at or after any celebration forms a part, is liable, on summary conviction, and so on. Can the minister inform the committee what has happened to make it necessary to make even that drastic wording more drastic still by the inclusion of these rather curiously worded phrases?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The difficulty, I am informed, exists among one particular tribe of Indians in British Columbia. The practice there has persisted and in many instances, according to the information I have, the Indians themselves get into very serious difficulties. The Indian has an idea of having a potlatch, and he begins to prepare for it. He may put hardship upon his family in order to accumulate the goods that he will give away when this ceremony takes place. I think it is only fair to say-and I believe that those in the house who are informed on the matter will agree with me-that the general doing away with the potlatch idea has been beneficial to the Indians as a whole. All evidence that I have been able to get confirms me in that view. In this particular amendment we are trying to strengthen the law. I have considerable respect for my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi, who was in the house many years ago while I was a member. The hon. gentleman thinks we have gone too far; but as I read this amendment it would have to be made very clear what the purpose was for which flour or sugar or something else was being accumulated, before conviction could be secured.
How can it be proved?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If it is not proved the Indian is not guilty.

Surely the act as it now stands sufficiently empowers the superintendent general. What the committee wants to know is what has happened recently to make it necessary for the superintendent general to strengthen his hand.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Representations have been made that this practice persists in one community in British Columbia, and the recommendation has come from the officers of the department that the law be strengthened in the manner proposed. I must frankly admit that I have no personal knowledge of the
Indian Act

matter, but on the representations made to me by the officials of the department and on evidence that has been submitted to me more in the form of letters from other interests who are sympathetic to the welfare of the Indians, I considered that the amendment was a proper one. I suggest that the committee accept it. I do not think that injustice to any Indian will result.

If injustice does not result it will be because the act is not enforced. Then what is the use of it? I agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), and I too would ask the minister what has happened to require this drastic change. I will ask him another question. He says that this has come to him on the recommendation of his officials, and of course the official with whom it originated is the Indian agent in the district concerned. How many years has that gentleman been Indian agent?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I regret very much that I am unable at the moment to give that information.

I am willing to supply it. He has been Indian agent for about two or possibly three years. I am familiar with his pedigree before that, and it did not suggest any intimacy with Indian affairs. Now that was the spirit in which this action originated. He recommends it to the commissioner, the commissioner recommends it to the deputy, and so it goes; but it started with the Indian agent. With all respect to that gentleman-I honour him as a Christian and esteem him as a brother countryman-I do say that he has not had very much experience as an Indian agent. The minister suggests trying out this legislation for two or three years; I would advise trying out that Indian agent for two or three years, and if at the end of that time he has not changed his opinion but still thinks that such a change as this is necessary, then the change may be made. If he does not agree then that the wise thing to do is to persuade the Indians to give up any excesses that may exist, instead of trying to attain that object by unjust and indefensible methods, then it will be time to make the change.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is that the agent at Alert Bay?
Yes; the minister knows about it.

I am in accord with the arguments of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. It is almost ridiculous to put on the statute boks a provision that will penalize a particular class of people merely because they
\ Mr. Crerar.]
are unfortunate enough not to be able to
protect themselves to a greater extent than they can at present. As has been pointed out they are liable to conviction merely for thinking or imagining something. If the principle of this legislation were put into force we should all be in gaol.

I strongly support the attitude of my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni. This provision should be left out of the bill. It is just possible that the Indian agent, who has been there a short time, wishes to show his zeal and has probably been prompted by commercial interests in the vicinity of the district in which the potlatch is held. I believe that if you went into the matter carefully you would discover that that was at the bottom of the whole idea. If a man spends his money with a certain firm and is therefore unable, having bought a lot of goods there, to spend money with a competing concern, there arises a difference which is brought to the attention of the Indian agent. By and large I am disposed to think that the Indians are correcting their own ideas of the past and assimilating rapidly those of the whites with whom they mix. I believe it would be better to leave the law as it was before this amendment was put forward.

If I can come to the
assistance of the minister to any extent I shall do so with pleasure. Section 13 in the explanatory notes, referring to this matter, states that particularly the more progressive elements among the Indians had had something to say about the form of certain parts of the Indian Act. May I ask the minister whether certain of the more progressive elements within the tribe concur with the Indian agent in suggesting the addition of these words?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes; they do. It is at their request.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot say definitely of
my own knowledge to what extent that is the case. But after all, may I draw the attention of the committee to the fact that the principle of suppressing any evils associated with the potlatch has been recognized in the law for over fifty years; and the provisions, as my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) pointed out a moment ago, have been rather stringent. All that this seeks to do is to-strengthen those provisions. While I am not a lawyer, I do not imagine that any justice-of the peace would convict an Indian under the amendment unless he had definite, clear evidence that he was accumulating these goods for the purpose of a potlatch. I can-

Indian Act
not see the force of the objections that have been raised by my hon. friends. As I have said, the amendment seeks to strengthen the section, and I think it will probably have that effect.

This is precisely
the kind of language that is used in a certain rather notorious piece of legislation, section 98 of the criminal code, to which some of us have in other connections strenuously objected. I believe it is good British law that a man is not charged with a crime until a crime has been committed. I object to a man being charged with crime before the crime is committed. This is what this clause of the amendment provides, that if a man is not only giving these goods away, but accumulating them with the thought that he might give them away, he is guilty of an offence. The word is definitely "before"- before any overt act takes place.
He accumulates those.

The accumulation
is a crime, the accumulation of goods with a view to doing something with them. I think it is bad law to make this a crime. My friend the hon. member for Selkirk, a former dean of the law school, is somewhat of an expert in this matter, and I stand to be corrected by him. But I think I am right in saying that the very essence of British law is that a man is not guilty until he has done some overt act. The same criticism arises, as has been pointed out by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill), in connection with the second clause of this amendment relating to a person suspected of being guilty of a certain thing. I do not like that. It does not seem to me that we ought to have a search warrant given merely on suspicion.	[DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
It has
always been that way.

In these days we
are going altogether too far in that line. Possibly in connection with some opium matters it may be necessary, although even with regard to such a matter I am always a little suspicious of this kind of legislation. But merely because a man is accumulating some goods or making some preparations does not, it seems to me, afford any real ground for giving a search warrant. You say: Well, this legislation applies to Indians. But even an Indian has inherent rights. We have had the same situation in connection with our labour movement. If a man is suspected the police can break into his house, look through his library and search his papers. I say that that kind of legislation is unfair
and un-British. The man is merely suspected of an offence. If it is found that he has been accumulating goods with the intention of giving them away a search warrant may be granted, but, as the member for Comox-Alberni has well put it, even a magistrate cannot say exactly what a man's intention is. Magistrates may be very expert, but they cannot X-ray a man's mind. But if it is thought that he has been accumulating with the intention of taking part in this ceremony, he is liable to have his goods seized. I do not think this is fair. The minister constantly urges that the idea is to do away with potlatch. Our criticism is not primarily related to the potlatch or to evils that allegedly go with it; our objection is to a type of legislation which, to some of us at least, seems absolutely un-British. I hope that the minister can see his way to withdraw this amendment.

I should like to comment on this from another point of view. Many Indians are collectors of furs and pelts for sale. Supposing a man has a number of these furs in his home, and he has an enemy- perhaps another Indian, perhaps a white man- although he may be a saving man, accumulating them to give to some of his sons and daughters when they get married, his enemy might whisper in the ear of the authorities: This is for a potlatch. Is it fair to expose the Indians to that risk by making these laws any more stringent? The present law is working well; the Indians are acting well; why add something that may be an irritant, may make the Indian dissatisfied, may create trouble for the law officers, and may entail additional cost in enforcing the law in many ways when there is no need for this? I do hope that the minister will reconsider this and not put the amendment into law.

May I appeal to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) on this point? It seems to me that we have discussed it for quite a while to-day; that there is a real difference of opinion on the subject, and that it had better stand for a little more information. The reason I suggest this is that the minister himself has stated that the old law has been working very well and that the abuses of this potlatch system have been gradually reduced. If that is the case, and we are gradually coming to the time when they will disappear, I am in accord with my hon. friend from Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) that it may be as well to leave well enough alone at the present time. At all events I think there should be some information before the committee as to the
Indian Act

frequency of this ceremony of potlatch twenty years ago, ten years ago, five years ago, and of recent date, to show whether there is a necessity for strengthening the law in this way. I think the Minister of Justice will consider that it is a severe provision to put into a statute to punish people for collecting goods for a purpose which they have in mind. It is going to be very hard for anybody to prove that that is their reason for collecting. I think the minister said that he did not know who the agent was in this particular locality who had made this recommendation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Unless the intent could be proved, no penalty would apply.

No. This recommendation came originally from the Indian agent out there, I take it; it has come through the department and has been put up to the minister through the officials of the department. The minister has told us more than once to-day that he has been in office such a short time that he has really not been able to get into touch with all these different matters. I suggest that he have the question gone into as to how the act has worked, and let us take this up again. He can then bring his official here in order that, if questions are asked, he will be able to supply any information which at present the minister does not possess.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am quite willing, if hon. members wish it, to let this clause stand. I do not know that very much additional information can be supplied respecting it.
Oh, yes, there must be.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As I have already indicated, this difficulty is confined practically to one instance in British Columbia where these celebrations persist. I think my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woods-worth) was a little far-fetched in the argument he advanced this afternoon. There is a real abuse in connection with this. Let me give my hon. friend an illustration. An Indian on the reserve may have a family. He decides to give a potlatch. He then commences to accumulate goods for that purpose; it may be flour; it may be sugar; it may be blankets; it may be anything, but his whole effort and attention are concentrated on the idea of collecting goods to give away. In the meantime there is real hardship on his family. After this event takes place in all likelihood his family are on public relief. It may be, as my hon. friend from Comox-Albemi has stated, that the proposed legislation is rather stringent, but it is simply extending the 
principle that has been in the law for fifty years, namely, to try to break down this practice among these Indians. I am quite willing, however, to let the clause stand.
Section stands.
On section 14-Who shall be deemed elected.

I should like to ask why the qualification necessary is the possession of a house. As I understand the matter, Indians on the reserve of which I have some knowledge do not own the land; that is the property of the band, but they do own the improvements on the land. An Indian may have a bam or fences or a good many other improvements on the property even though he does not have a house on it. He may live on the next farm, but under this section he must own a house and have it on his property before he is eligible for election to council. It seems to me that some other qualification should be the deciding factor with regard to an Indian's qualifications for election to council.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know whether my hon. friend has read the explanatory note accompanying this section, but that sets out very clearly the purpose of the amendment.
Mr, SENN: That does not answer the question. I quite understand that for many years the provision has been that an Indian must own a house on the reserve before being eligible for election to council. He may have a barn or fences or other improvements on a good farm within the reserve, but the house may be on the next farm that he has rented. That makes him ineligible for election to council. If he has other property equivalent in value to a house I do not see why he should be debarred from becoming a councillor. I would suggest that a property qualification such as the municipalities have, to the amount of say, $400 of personal property or real estate, would be a better arrangement, but I do not think it fair to make it incumbent upon a man to possess that one particular qualification of owning a house.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The suggestion of my hon. friend would necessitate a further amendment to the act. At the present time an Indian who desires to qualify as a councillor has not only to be possessed of a house on the reserve but also to live in the house. By this amendment we seek to effect a change so that while he will have to own a house on the reserve, it will not be necessary for him to live in that particular house in order to qualify as a councillor.

Supply-Agriculture-Dairying
I quite understand that.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It makes it easier for him to qualify for the position.

I quite understand that it makes it easier for him to qualify as a councillor, but I cannot understand why he must have this particular qualification. He might own other property far more valuable than a house; he might have vested interests in the band; he might have other qualifications such as education, experience and good judgment, but even though he possess all these other qualifications, if he does not own a house he cannot qualify for council. It seems to me that the minister might very well consider some other method.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I might say that this has been the law for a great many years, and no instances of hardship have come to my notice. While I appreciate very much the observations of the hon. gentleman in connection with the matter he has drawn to my attention, I do not think it is really as important as he thinks it is.

speechtext:
Section agreed to.

May I bring to the attention of the committee the fact that very often the farmers suffer because they have not enough cold storage warehouses. They have to sell their butter to intermediaries, or inbetween merchants in the larger cities. If a farmer could have the advantage of a cold storage warehouse he could keep the butter from the season when it sells at a low price until the fall and winter months when it sells at a higher rate, thereby deriving the benefit of storing for a few months. I suggest that this would be a paying proposition. At a meeting in Riviere du Loup I advocated this principle before -the provincial Minister of Agriculture. At that point a cold storage plant has been built with the help of the Department of Agriculture. It was built to serve a good purpose, but unfortunately the attention of the farmers has not been directed to its use; they do not realize that by the investment of a small amount of money in cold storage facilities they could store two carloads of butter which would give them a clear profit of at least $6,000 at the end of the year.
We must regret that the profit is made not by the farmer, as is the case in other countries, but by the go-between at the expense of the farmer and -the consumer. If bu-tter were kept in warehouses belonging to cooperative butter producing farmers both they and the consumers would benefit. The consumer could buy butter at a cheaper rate later in the year. Last year when I drew this matter to the attention of the minister's illustrious predecessor I did not receive a satisfactory reply; in fact I did not receive any during the last five years. speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, March 17, ' consideration of the motion of Mr. Boulanger for the second reading of Bill No. 9, to amend the Civil Service Act (vacancies, outside service, priority of returned soldiers).

When I was interrupted the other evening I was trying to prove that the Civil Service Act had not had the benefit of cooperation from the former Conservative government. On that occasion I was discussing the position of lightkeeper, which carries a salary of S150 a year. Any position with a salary greater than that comes under the civil service commission. Though I was not able to recommend a man for that position I was asked to recommend a man for a postmastership entailing a salary of $2,000 a year or thereabouts. In my opinion the act as it now stands is not uniform; it confuses me and probably other members as well, for I do not know what positions actually do come under the
commission. I suggest to the present government that the act should be made more uniform. If positions are to be under the civil service commission a definite limit in regard to salary should be established. I made certain allegations with regard to abuses that had crept into the act, and I think, in view of these allegations, we should decide upon some method whereby the abuses may be removed.
I believe that the Civil Service Act is a remarkable one; the merit system is to be commended. I would point out, however, that Canada is a vast country and conditions here are different from conditions in England. I admit that in Great Britain any candidate or any member of parliament who suggested to the civil service commission there the appointment of any particular person to a position would be ruined. But, I repeat, this is a vast country. The commission is located at Ottawa and thousands of miles away it becomes necessary to appoint someone to the position of lightkeeper, with a salary of $150 a year. Is it sensible to send an examiner all the way from Ottawa to hold an oral examination in order to appoint that man? It does not seem sensible. The former government saw fit to increase the revenue limit in connection with post offices to $3,000 a year, and we have had no trouble in appointments under $3,000, so that probably that would be a reasonable basis on which to make these appointments.
I was not able to read the whole of it, because it is quite long, but I did read parts of an excellent report prepared by the late Hon. James Malcolm in 1923. It was one of the most remarkable reports ever presented in connection with the Civil Service Act, and it is well worth reading. It sets out certain evils and recommends amendments that would be beneficial. In my opinion a member of parliament should be at liberty to speak to the commission with regard to any appointment that is to be made in his riding. As a member I do not think I should have to sneak through the back door to speak to the commission; I do not think I should be placed in that position.
In this large country and with conditions such as they are to-day, I believe that every member is interested in the poor man. The member realizes that any small position that can be given is helpful, and he wishes to assist the poorer classes, for they are the ones that need help; and no one knows these people better than does the member. I am speaking now of the $150 job, which would be of assistance to any poor man 'and his family. Certain qualifications are
Civil Service Act

necessary if a man is to fill the position of lightkeeper satisfactorily, but there is in my riding a man of seventy-seven who has that position. I have not one word to say against 'him; he is an honourable man. But he is seventy-seven and somebody else has to light the lights for him; yet he is supposedly in active service to-day. Obviously, therefore, an age limit is necessary. Under the Civil Service Act I believe it is sixty-five, but apparently that is not quite satisfactory because you will find order in council after order in council setting aside that particular provision in respect of certain appointments. The act might be amended to fix the limit at seventy years.
I submit that the member should be notified before any appointment is actually made in his riding. I do not say that he should have patronage altogether, but he should first be notified, and if he has reason to argue with the commission against the advisability of appointing anyone he should be heard. For, after all, he is elected by the people of that particular riding and he knows the conditions. Our situation is different from that in Great Britain. There some 500 members or more represent a very small island, while in Canada 245 members represent a very wide territory, and the members of the civil service commission do not know the people personally. Therefore, with respect to any of these small positions in any riding I suggest that the member should be notified before the appointment is actually made, and if he has any particular objection he ought to be able to go to the commission and say so. I do not think that he should have to sneak through the back door. That is not right.
I do not believe in the whole bill. I do not believe that we should open our whole outside service to patronage; I think to do so would be a disaster. I have in mind one instance in the post office service, in respect of the rural mail service, which is apparently the outside service. The man I have in mind gave perfect service immediately after this election. I intended to rectify what the former defeated Conservative candidate did in that riding in the last five years. The official concerned spent two hours with me; he knew every mail route in my riding, and he gave me valuable assistance. But a great many little appointments could easily be left to the member for the riding. This would save this country a great deal of expense; it would avoid all the red tape which a man has to go through to-day in connection with these small appointments, and for which not he, but the whole country has to pay. Think how easy it is to make one of these small appointments

directly through the member; it is only a matter of one letter; whereas if an appointment goes through the civil service commission it has to pass through about one dozen channels; I counted them; I looked through them in connection with the Malcolm report, where they had them set out. We could save that money, and we have to save money to-day.
I do not agree with this bill as it is printed, but it has certain merits. I am willing to take the word of the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) that the government is not accepting the principle of the bill, but that he desires that it go to a committee to be studied. I am anxious that some method be found whereby we can take the canker spots from the Civil Service Act, because certain provisions of the act as it stands remind me of a provision of the election act whereby no candidate is allowed to pay for cabs for hauling voters to the polls; nobody respects that provision. That is exactly the position in this case. Until you have an act which the people respect you cannot enforce it. The present act is like the Ontario Temperance Act in that respect. That is why I desire that the act shall be amended so that the people will respect it, I cannot make them respect it the way it is to-day. I ask that, if possible, it be referred to a committee and' be amended.

Because the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) has had the courage to introduce this bill and to discuss it in the even manner in which he has discussed it, he is criticized for his independence.
There is another matter which surprised me in the course of the hon. member's address. He was greatly concerned for the future of the Liberal party. He made a direct appeal to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King). He then singled out the members of the government one after another; then he made a direct appeal to us who emanate from western Canada, and after that he gave a warning to the whole of the rest of the Liberal party, and, in addition, a little course of instruction to us, as new members, on what we were expected to do and what might be done. Then he went on to state:
Yesterday we had the spectacle in the house of the Prime Minister telling the members that 12739-84
they must not vote for an amendment that would mean a lower tariff on agricultural implements.
It may not be part of my responsibility, Mr. Speaker, to refer to that in the presence of the Prime Minister; I know he will take care of that statement himself. But I was in the house at that time, and as I understood the Prime Minister's remark, it was not an instruction that we must not do something; he was pointing out what had been repeated time and again on the floor of this chamber, namely, that if the Canada-United States agreement was to pass this house it had to be accepted in its entirety, and for that reason a motion for the free entry of agricultural implements could not then be accepted but could be discussed after the budget was introduced. Then the hon. gentleman went on, and this is the part that concerns me most as a private member and as a supporter of the Liberal party:
There can be no threat held b5r the Prime Minister or any member of the government over private members for standing up for what I think a great many of them really believe, and for what I know a great many of their constituents really believe.
In my short experience I have had the privilege of sitting as a supporter of three Liberal premiers, all three of whom are members of this house at the present time. Never on any occasion during the eight years I was in the provincial house of Saskatchewan was anything in the nature of a threat held out by any Liberal premier with whom I had the pleasure of being associated, and I may say that that is absolutely true also so far as the distinguished leader of our party, the present Prime Minister of Canada, is concerned. Nothing like that was ever suggested to us; we were given absolute freedom of thought and of expression, to espouse or to oppose any measure according to our own inclinations. The only responsibility that we were ever asked to observe was that if we intended to oppose any government measure we should be good enough to tell the whip of our intention. Nothing could be fairer than that. I think the Prime Minister, the present leader of the Liberal party, would have some cause for concern, worry and disapproval if he thought the members supporting him in this house gave their support to any measure because of any inclination, thought or action of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth). The hon. member referred to "what I think a great many of them really believe," and "what I know a great many of their constituents really believe." I do deprecate such a contention as that put forward by the hon.

Civil Service Act

member and I think that his strictures are of even greater importance than the principle of this particular bill.
The civil service has been in the maelstrom of politics ever since confederation. From 1868 to 1882 no fewer than four royal commissions were appointed in Canada for the purpose of making surveys and reports on the civil service. In 1877 Mr. Cayley, then a member of this house, introduced a measure sponsoring very wide spread reforms and the introduction of the merit system, but though his measure passed the house nothing came of it. In 1882 another royal commission was appointed, because the government of the day had come to the conclusion that there were not enough governmental positions to accommodate the whole male population of the country. That is pretty much the situation to-day. Again in 1891 a royal commission was appointed to make a survey of the civil service, but nothing came of it. Then in 1893 there was a change of government and matters continued in pretty much the same way until 1907, because from 1896 to 1907 there was a wave of prosperity throughout the country made possible by the application of Liberal principles and policies. In 1907 another royal commission was appointed to investigate and report on the civil service, and in 1908, following that report, a civil service act was introduced and the first civil service commission was established in Canada. It is true that the Civil Service Act of that day did not extend to the outside service, but it did cover the inside service. In 1911 there was a change of government, and between September, 1911, and 1914 there were no less than 11,000 dismissals from the civil service. So great was the disruption of the service due to the conduct of the government of that day that they deemed it wise to appoint still another royal commission in 1912 or 1913. The war broke out before any action could be taken on the report of that commission. Finally in 1918 the present Civil Service Act was passed, and it has been the law of this land ever since. I agree with many hon. members who have spoken thus far, that there is much of merit in the present Civil Service Act, but that is no reason why this house should not now investigate the ramifications of that act and its application to our far-flung dominion, and endeavour to improve it.
Reference has been made to a good many things that have happened in the application of that act. One provision that meets with popular disapproval is that applicants are required to sit for an examination and to pay a fee of one dollar. In one case there
[Mr. D. A. McNiven.J
were ninety-three applicants for a particular position; each applicant paid one dollar; one man obtained the appointment and ninety-two were advised that they were on the eligible list. Within a year that eligible list was cancelled and ninety-two people were disappointed. In my own city one position in the weights and measures branch remained vacant from April of 1931, another from July of 1934 and a third from July of 1935. All three positions were filled in August and September of last year, just before the election. About two weeks before October 14 an official who had presided over a department in the city of Regina was removed from that department and brought to Ottawa and an Ottawa man was sent west to take his place. Nobody knows what the reason was; nobody has yet been able to ascertain it. That situation was corrected.
I refer to this matter only as an indication, along with some of the other observations that have been made, that there is much that should be investigated and much that might be improved.
I had not intended to take as much time as I have, but before I sit down I would like to join with other hon. members who have already spoken in paying homage and respect to the Canadian soldier. It is little enough to do for the Canadian soldier to maintain that preference which he enjoys under the present act. At the same time I am not at all sure that the Canadian soldier would ask that the act be administered so as to exclude the Imperial. When we go to the senate chamber and look at that magnificent painting depicting the landing of the first British troops in France, and when we think of the exploits of the "Contemptibles," their heroism displayed at Mons, this country should show them every regard and give them every consideration in its public service. Also we must remember that following the war, by a concerted plan of both governments Imperial returned men were encouraged to come to this country. At the present time I know a man who is applying for a position, who was in the navy for the whole of the four war years, who was a member of the crew of a convoy ship that convoyed Canadian troops from our shores to Great Britain and France, who was actually torpedoed and whose ship was sunk, and who came to this country at our invitation. I would not like to see anything incorporated in our act that Would exclude a man who has given such splendid service to the empire from any position for which his merit qualifies him.
We have a good civil service, and the permanency Of that service is something which

will benefit the Canadian people. The public conies into daily contact with these men, and is entitled to the very best service that can be given in the administration of the affairs of this country.
I have already expressed my opposition to the principle of this bill, for the reasons I have stated, and I wish to affirm again that if it is possible to have the Civil Service Act and the officials who are administering it brought before a committee of this house I would gladly give that the full measure of my support.

Before the vote is taken on this motion there are a few words that I wish to say. First, I want to thank the hon. member for Belle-chasse (Mr. Boulanger) for the way he introduced this bill, because he stated clearly and definitely its objects. That makes the discussion much easier. He said that the bill has four objects in view: First, to place the outside civil service beyond the control of the civil service commission, and, second, to make it obligatory for the civil service commission to consult heads of departments before making appointments or promotions, in order that the last word in making such appointments or promotions may be with the heads of departments and not with the commission. I would ask hon. members when considering this bill to have regard to the citizens and taxpayers, the people of Canada. There are millions of taxpayers many of whom are in areas in which there are hardly any civil servants, but they contribute to the salaries of the civil service, and they look to the civil service of Canada to be above politics. When they have occasion to visit any public office I am glad to say that for the most part they are received by the civil servants there with courtesy and given what information they need, and they usually find the civil service capable.
But if this bill is passed in its present form and the objects as described by the hon. member who introduced it are achieved, what will be the result? The bill means definitely that the minister of each department will make the appointments; no other meaning can be taken from it. I feel sorry for the ministers, for, peculiar as it may seem, Conservatives have sometimes a little sympathy with Liberal ministers, as I hope at times Liberals have with Conservative ministers. After trying for fifteen or twenty years to build up an efficient civil service in this country, why should we tear it down completely and destroy it and
12739-Mj
Civil Service Act
cause the people of Canada to lose their faith and confidence in parliamentary measures?
This bill deals with promotion. It would mean that many civil servants who had hoped to work their way up in the service would see someone brought in from the outside-
That is what they did.
I quite appreciate that the hon. gentleman's party might do it.
You did it.
And I give them full credit for it.
We did not do it.

You have a majority now and it is your privilege to enforce this measure. Your party was in power from 1921 to 1930; why did you not make these changes then that are now suggested by a private member?
The effect of this legislation on the efficiency of the civil service can readily be understood. What would the older members of the civil service think who, after years of service, saw an outsider advanced past them? What new man ever came into any office who understood the details of his work until he was trained by someone ahead of him or someone completely informed on all points? Then there is another consideration; new men would receive the appointments whether the commission had recommended them or not. It is not the duty of the ministers to make appointments; they may have that privilege through a party majority, but they must use it carefully and honestly when they exercise it. The civil service of Canada has just begun to be recognized as an important asset of the dominion, and the changes proposed in this bill would tend to destroy it. If those changes have to be made I ask the government to assume the responsibility. If they believe in the principles of the bill, let them show this by making the bill a government measure. Then those of us who are fearful that the civil service may be made less efficient will at least have the responsibility taken from our shoulders and we will not be parties to the destruction of that service.
What of merit all along the line; how are you to decide? I have a little experience in political affairs. I know positions vacant in my constituency are now being filled by Liberals. I do not objeet; that is the privilege of the party in power; the people gave
Civil Service Act

them a mandate permitting them to do so, but that is no reason why I should support a measure destroying the civil service of Canada.
I wonder what hon. members representing the city of Ottawa think about this measure. When I have seen the corridors of this building crowded and I have thought of the position of those members, I was at least sympathetic enough to thank providence that there was a civil service commission, if only for their sake.
I am prepared to oppose the bill. I have a feeling that the Liberal party will carry it out in detail. They have a large majority, and I hope they will not abuse it in any way by making changes in the act. I do not believe they will. For these reasons I oppose the principle of the bill.

Mr. Speaker, underlying the activities of any government should be high ideals, and those ideals should develop an excellent civil service. We have a Civil Service Act which has been in operation for many years but which under certain circumstances has been found to be faulty. The obvious procedure is to improve the act and the conduct of officials obeying it. We can point to countries with an excellent civil service operating under a Civil Service Act. On the other hand we cannot point to any country not operating under a Civil Service Act which has high ideals among its service.
In my view the throwing over of the Civil Service Act as we now have it would be a directly retrograde movement, and we cannot permit ourselves to go backward. There is no excuse for turning the civil service into a "swivel" service, and for that reason I am definitely opposed to the bill.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill
introduced by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger), like many other measures, has some provisions which are commendable and, judging from expressions by hon. members in different parts of the house, provisions which are commended generally. There are other provisions, however, which I think are quite the opposite. Personally I do not approve that portion of the bill which proposes to take the outside service from under the control of the civil service commission. I have been long enough in public life to know, after following discussions in parliament after parliament with respect to the civil service, how difficult it has been to regulate the service in a manner which will secure both efficiency and security. I believe what in

these respects has been accomplished under the Civil Service Act as regards both inside and outside services has been in the main in the right direction. There is no doubt, however, that as it stands the act is not perfect; obviously it needs amendment in some particulars. If it had been perfect many of the complaints made in this chamber about what has been done even within the last few years would not have been possible.
My hon. friend and colleague the Secretary of State (Mr. Rinfret) suggested an evening or two ago that it might be well without prejudice to have the bill referred to a committee for study. That is frequently done with respect to measures introduced in parliament. It has been understood by all parties that the purpose of such committee would be one primarily of study and report, and that no hon. member or party would be regarded as approving or disapproving the principle of the bill so long as the deliberations in committee were proceeded with on that understanding. However, in view of the difference of opinion which exists with respect to the wisdom of that course it may be as well to forego any idea of pursuing it further. I feel that it would be to the advantage of hon. members to have a chance to study the Civil Service Act in a committee of the house, and to consider possible amendments thereto. I make that statement for this, among other reasons, that in the present House of Commons we have a large number of new members, and I believe that if an opportunity were given for a full study of the act many features which to-day may not be understood would be understood more clearly. Furthermore, we are living in times when, in different directions, there is much in the way of change. Unquestionably there is room for improvement in the act and for bringing the provisions more into conformity with what many of us may feel is essential in these times. Having this in mind and having discussed the matter with my colleagues I would say that at the next session of parliament the government proposes to invite the house to constitute a special select committee to study the Civil Service Act, to investigate its provisions, and to give to the committee power to make recommendations to the house. That would fulfil a purpose which, I believe, is essential, and one which will certainly have to be carried out at some session of this parliament.
I do not think there has been a parliament in the last ten years which has not appointed a committee or a commission to study the Civil Service Act, and perhaps it would be just as well if this parliament did not prove to be

Supply-Itulian Affairs
the exception. I do not think it would be advisable to take that step at this session because already we have a very large number of committees. Almost all hon. members are already on some committees, and unless this session continues until the fall-which I hope it wrill not-perhaps we would do well not to add to the number.
While I would be prepared personally to give a measure of support to certain of the provisions of the bill, I would certainly strongly oppose anything in the direction of getting away from the merit system in connection with the great body of the public service in Canada. That view is shared by the government, and if, after what I have just said, we must decide the matter without having the bill withdrawn then, certainty, I for one shall oppose a second reading and hope that the government will be supported in its attitude.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
DEPARTMENT OF INDIAN AFFAIRS Indians-
To provide for expenses connected with the administration of Indian Affairs, including salaries, supplies, relief, medical attendance, hospitalization, dwellings, agricultural activities, surveys, roads, bridges, irrigation, dyking, education, et cetera, and a grant of $100,000 approved by parliament in the session of 1926-27, $4,241,100.
I only rise to ask if the estimates of the Department of Indian Affairs have been before the committee already?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Superintendent General of Indian Affaire):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes; this item was under discussion, but the committee reported progress before the item was passed. On that occasion the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Perley) asked for information respecting Indian doctors in Saskatchewan. There is a total of eighteen attendants employed for Indians in that province, all but two of whom are engaged for part-time attendance. One of the two full-time medical officers is at Fort Qu'Appelle, having charge of Qu'Appelle and the File Hills Indian agencies, and the other full-time officer is at Battleford in charge of the Battleford Indian agency. The Indians of Saskatchewan have also an oportunity of sharing in the benefits and the service of the departmental eye specialist for the diagnosis of trachoma, and the specialist also advises the local medical officers as to how the disease should be treated.
On what terms are the part-time medical officers employed?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Some of the part-time
doctors are on what is known as the call system, while others are part-time officers appointed by the civil service commission.

Would the minister be kind enough to inform me if instructions have been given lately by the department to the Indian agent at Cacouna to stop payment of the small monthly allowance of S6.10 to the Indians in the district from Riviere du Loup onwards. I have a few Indians in Rimouski, and I have been informed that this small monthly payment has been stopped for a month or so. I would like to know whether instructions have been given from headquarters at Ottawa to that effect.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Was that for relief allowances.

It was for relief allowance. I have one Indian in mind, a man named Bois, of Mont Job. I wrote the department, but did not get an answer. The
Supply-Indian Affairs

agent of the Indian department, Mr. Lebel, at Cacouna, informed the man that by instruction of the department at Ottawa the allowance he had been receiving of S6 a month had been stopped. I have had other inquiries from other Indians in the county of Rimouski, all of whom report the same thing, that the monthly payment had been stopped on instructions from the Superintendent General of Indian Affairs at Ottawa to his agent, Mr. Lebel, of Cacouna, county of Temiscouata, Quebec.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry that I have not the information before me, nor has my deputy, but I assure my hon. friend that the matter will be looked into immediately.
If the information is sent to me I shall be satisfied.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If any hardship has been done it will be corrected.
Can the minister give any information with respect to the nurses employed at the different agencies? Have the full-time medical officers nurses assisting them?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The doctor in charge of Qu'Appelle and the File Hills agencies has the assistance of a public health nurse. I cannot say at the moment just what number of nurses are employed among the Indians in Saskatchewan.
Is there a fulltime nurse on the Crooked Lake reserve?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am informed by my deputy that the nurse who was on that reserve has been removed to Norway House. Her place will be taken by another nurse because it is the intention to have a full-time nurse there.

What sort of
supervision is exercised over the part-time doctors? I have a complaint from the Cowichan reserve that the doctors pay only perfunctory attention to their patients. For instance, a doctor was telephoned on Thursday and arrived on Saturday at eleven p.m. the case was an urgent one and the patient, a child, is now in hospital. That seems to be rather a case of neglect than anything else.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know the circumstances. It is impossible to keep in touch with all these cases, but I can tell the hon. gentleman that if at any time he has any complaint in respect of a matter of this kind I shall be grateful if he will bring it to my attention and I will see that it is remedied
[Sir Eugem* Fiset.J
if possibLe. The doctor who is on part-time is supposed to discharge his duties properly, and if he is failing to do so we shall probably discharge him and get somebody else.

Thank you
That is one of a large number of complaints which I submitted to the minister's department some weeks ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I must say that at the
moment I cannot fully answer the question, but it will be looked into.

When a doctor is
called to see a patient does he follow up the case as he would with his other patients, or is he brought in again only when he is called? The doctor may be called to see a patient suffering from pneumonia and give treatment, going away after telling the attendants what is wrong, and he may not return until called again five or six days afterwards when perhaps the patient is about to pass out. He has never had an opportunity to do anything with the patient. Are the doctors required to go back from time to time after the first visit just as they would with other patients?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Yes; I am informed that
the doctor is supposed to look after these patients the same as he would any other patient of his own. If he visits a patient and finds him suffering from pneumonia and thinks it necessary to pay another visit the following day or even the same day it is his duty to do so. That is what he is paid for.

What is the reason
for this considerable decrease of 8252,000 in the allotment for Indians this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The only answer is, in
the name of economy. We have endeavoured to keep our estimates as low as we reasonably can. I should like to have seen this vote larger, but we are trying to get along as economically as possible.

In what respects is
economy being effected? The times are trying for the Indians because they cannot get additional work. On the reservation in my constituency they are quite hard up.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
We have effected a small
economy in administration. We have made a reduction with regard to new equipment for residential schools, having decided to get along with the old equipment, and that accounts for $48,200. We have also cut down the amount for new residential schools, which accounts for over $75,000. There is also a

Supply-Indian Affairs
reduction in the amount for new day school buildings. Some of the old day schools should be replaced by newer schools, but we are going to try to get along with the old ones. Then there is an item of repairs to residential schools, which amounts to $6,000.

Has there been any
reduction in salaries?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.

What is the policy of the department in the matter of hospitalization? Have the doctors who are on call the power to direct in any case that a patient shall go to a particular hospital? There are nine reserves in the constituency of Qu'Appelle and we have two or three pretty good municipal hospitals, one at Indian Head and a small one at Whitewood. Very often Indians are taken past these municipal hospitals into Regina, either to the general hospital or the Grey Nuns' hospital. The people who keep up the municipal hospitals think the Indians should not be taken past their door to Regina, and I make a [DOT] special plea for these local hospitals. The one at Indian Head is a particularly good hospital which would serve well. Does the doctor direct to which hospital the patient is to be taken or does the department do so?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The practice has been to
take the Indian to the hospital to which he prefers to go. The hospital at Indian Head would probably not be equipped for major operations. I do not know, but I am informed that in order to get the best medical attention where serious operations are necessary patients are taken to those points at which the best medical skill is available.

The hospital
at Indian Head is equipped with X-ray machines and it is adequately equipped for major operations. I know in many instances the doctors direct that these patients be taken past Indian Head to Regina, and this is a grievance on the part of the municipality. What progress are the specialists in the department making in stamping out trachoma? They have been doing a good deal of work on the Crooked Lake reserve and I should like to know how they are getting along.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I understand that a good deal of progress is being made in eradicating trachoma. There is no doubt that a good deal more progress could be made if we had the money to spend on medical care and education of these Indians in proper sanitary measures,
but I think reasonable progress is being made with the money that we have at our disposal. The situation is improving; it is not as bad as it was.

I see in this vote provision is made for dwellings. The dwelling at the Indian agency in the Crooked Lake reserve was burned down, I think two or three years ago. They have never rebuilt there. At the present time the agent is living in, I think, the town of Broadview, which is ten or twelve miles or more from the agency. Is the department considering rebuilding? It is quite an inconvenience for the agent to be such a distance from the reserve, especially in the winter time, as it is then impossible for him to drive. Is any provision being made for rebuilding?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid that no provision is being made this year for the residence of which my hon. friend speaks. It may be possible next year to consider it.
How much is being paid per month for relief to the Indians?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know that I can give the information by months to my hon. friend, but my officials say that the total bill for relief this year will probably be around $900,000.
I mean individually. How much do they get per capita?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I should think that varies in various places.

It is unfortunate that in the reserve in my riding only $4 per month is paid to the head of a family, and it appears quite immaterial whether the head of a family has eight or nine or only two in his family to look after. Four dollars is very little, even for an Indian.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It would act as a discouragement to large families, would it not?
It would seem to, but I am afraid it won't.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is no fixed scale. I understand that the practice is to try to meet the needs as far as reasonably can be done.

I should like to ask a question regarding the duties of the medical officers at the different Indian reserves. Take, for instance, the case where the medical officer is not a qualified surgeon and an emergency surgical operation is necessary on an Indian
Supply

Indian Affairs

patient. Is it the duty of the medical officer to engage a qualified surgeon and to pay that surgeon out of his own pocket, or will the department pay the surgeon?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: In such cases as the hon. member mentions the practice has been for the department to pay the surgeon's fees. I might say that the principle underlying the whole medical administration is that the Indians shall be well looked after in a medical way. If there is a doctor who is not a surgeon, and he discovers an Indian who should have his appendix out, his business is to get that Indian somewhere where he can have his appendix taken out safely. In such a case the department looks after the charge. But I believe it is the practice to have those charges taxed where in the judgment of the medical officers of the department at Ottawa they should be taxed. At any rate the aim is to give the proper attention to the Indians.

I should like to call the attention of the minister to the head office for Indian Affairs in British Columbia. It is in a very old building. All the records of the Indian department for British Columbia are kept in that building. If there should be a fire-and there have been one or two incipient fires-the result may be imagined in view of the fact that the building is heated by coal and wood stoves and is a wooden structure without even a fireproof vault for keeping the records. I want to leave that thought with the minister in the hope that he may be able to do something towards getting into the new building there which is under contemplation. I wish further to ask with regard to amounts voted for the education of Indian children; I believe that is divided between various religious denominations in British Columbia. Could the minister name the different religious bodies and the amount which was voted to each one last year, if your records are complete for one fiscal year?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
In reply to the first observation made by the hon. member, I am afraid that his criticism is only too true. The administration building in British Columbia is not what it should be, but I hope to have an opportunity of looking over it some time during the summer, and we shall certainly keep that in mind. Again may I say that there are many things we should like to do in the Indian administration, but we are proceeding with as much regard to economy as we can.
With regard to the other question, I may be able to give my hon. friend some informa-

tion, although not so complete, perhaps, as he desires. I find that at the Ahousaht school, under the United Church, the allowance for
1936-37 is estimated at SI 1,700; at Albemi, under the United Church, it is $20,700; at Alert Bay, where the Anglican church has a school, the total amount is $36,000; and at Cariboo, where the Roman Catholics have charge of the school, the amount is $22,950. In the first three instances that represents a per capita allowance of $180; in the last at Cariboo, the per capita is $170.
Will the minister kindly give the figures for the Coqualeetza and St. Mary's schools?
Possibly the minister would send me a list of them?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I find that the per capita allowance in the various schools runs from $170 to $180. I must here pay a tribute to all these denominations in respect of the educational work they are carrying on among the Indians. They are certainly performing a splendid service, and I venture to say that very often they carry on under considerable difficulties. I hope to cooperate with them as fully as possible because, after all, as far as my observation has gone, I think sound educational methods among these Indians are very helpful.

The reason I have asked this question is because I have had many inquiries in this connection, and to some extent the suggestion has been that one school is conducted better than another. I have visited one or two and found them very satisfactory; I have no reason to believe that suggestion is true, so I have asked the minister to give me the fullest information possible so that I may intelligently speak to those who inquire of me. If there is any further information the minister could give me I would appreciate it.
